evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: So one question that I have is around just broadly speaking what makes for a compelling pitch? I hear what you're saying about how you can really improve somebody's technical pitch, make it sound really good, but I think as someone who has pitched thousands of people, a much bigger part, I feel, is around messaging in the right way to the right person.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: And every pitch can be tailored slightly differently to cater more towards a particular person.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: So how do you think about that?

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: I think, you know, to Jillian's point, even let's just take this room, for example, // even though we're all investors and all investors of the same stage, we have all had very different experiences in pitching different kinds of people or receiving different kinds of pitches and that has shaped our beliefs about // what should go into a pitch and all of that. And I think it is even really challenging to even, let's say, pitch this pitch in the most optimal way to five people who generally have the same archetype.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: I think it's like, how do you get the right angle on the messaging? Like, I -

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: How do you think about the market? Because I think - you know, as someone who previously worked at an accelerator, budgets are pretty tight. So - and I realize the price point is affordable but like how do you kind of make that really compelling for these organizations?

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: What does it take to onboard a university? You know, when I think universities, I also cringe because I feel like, gosh, oh, they're so high touch, and your price point is only whatever, $40 a month.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: The part I'm struggling with is this, I can see why with this, people can win pitch competitions. It's like, I need to come up with a two-minute pitch that's really compelling to a broad audience. Great. // But with sales, it's more dynamic. I am - I'm not going in and talking at somebody for five minutes and that's that.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: It's we're having back and forth conversation -

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: And so does this tool help with that?

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: But best in class, just to be clear, is based on your experts grading and saying this sounds -

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: I think my challenge is I fund so many companies with terrible pitches that it's actually only partly the pitch, but also the actual idea and the messaging again catered towards the right investor is what matters more.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: I can understand that. // But I think where I'm landing on this is ultimately a pitch is not just about the most optimal structure // I think, the angle and the messaging you go in with is very personal and you don't know that until you actually meet with the person and you discover more information in the conversation along the way. So it's quite dynamic.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: So maybe this can get you in the door, but I feel like to close is so much more and -

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: And then I think, my last thought is, if - then if you can't kind of close most of that way, I wonder what sort of, you know, strong value people get out of this to - to stay retained over time. And so as such, I'm going to be out.

She also questions organizational willingness to pay and high-touch university onboarding, culminating in an explicit concern that insufficient closing value may undermine retention.
